title: Euclid's Theorem: Infinitely Many Primes

statement.text: Prove that there are infinitely many prime numbers.

objectives: Apply proof by contradiction to number theory
Recognize why this proof technique is powerful

currentState.expression: We want to prove: There are infinitely many primes.
currentState.description: How should we approach this proof?

prompt.question: Which proof technique is most suitable for this theorem?
prompt.hint: It's hard to construct all infinitely many primes directly. What if we assume there are only finitely many?

options.text: Proof by contradiction: Assume there are finitely many primes
Direct proof: List all the primes
Proof by induction on the number of primes

correct.explanation: Perfect! We'll assume there are only finitely many primes and derive a contradiction. This is Euclid's classical approach from around 300 BCE.
correct.insight: Proof by contradiction is often powerful for proving existence of infinite sets.

incorrect.1: We can't list infinitely many primes directly. This approach won't work for proving infinitude.
incorrect.2: Induction works for statements indexed by natural numbers, but 'infinitely many' isn't structured that way.

currentState.expression: Assume for contradiction that there are finitely many primes.
currentState.description: If there are finitely many, we can list them all.

prompt.question: If there are finitely many primes, how can we denote them?
prompt.hint: We can list them in a finite sequence.

options.text: Let $p_1, p_2, p_3, \ldots, p_n$ be all the prime numbers
Let $p$ be the largest prime number
Let $2, 3, 5, 7$ be all the primes

correct.explanation: Excellent! We assume there are exactly $n$ primes and list them all. This notation allows us to work with the complete set.
correct.insight: A finite set can always be enumerated as $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$.

incorrect.1: While there might be a largest prime in our assumption, listing all of them gives us more to work with.
incorrect.2: We don't want to specify which primes they are. We want a general argument that works for any finite list.

currentState.expression: We have all primes: $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$
currentState.description: Euclid's clever idea: construct a new number using these primes.

prompt.question: Consider the number $N = p_1 \cdot p_2 \cdot p_3 \cdots p_n + 1$. What can we say about N?
prompt.hint: Think about what happens when you divide N by any of the primes $p_i$.

options.text: $N$ is not divisible by any of $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$
$N$ is divisible by $p_1$
$N$ is equal to one of the primes

correct.explanation: Perfect! When we divide $N$ by any $p_i$, we get remainder 1 (since $N = (p_1 \cdots p_n) + 1$). So no $p_i$ divides $N$.
correct.insight: This is the key insight: N is constructed to leave remainder 1 when divided by each prime in our list.

incorrect.1: Not quite. If $p_1 | N$, then $p_1 | (N - p_1 \cdot p_2 \cdots p_n) = 1$, which is impossible.
incorrect.2: N is much larger than all the primes in our list (it's their product plus 1).

currentState.description: Every integer greater than 1 has at least one prime divisor.

prompt.question: What does the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic tell us about N?
prompt.hint: Every integer $n > 1$ is either prime or has a prime divisor.

options.text: $N$ is either prime itself, or has a prime divisor
$N$ must be composite
$N$ has no prime divisors

correct.explanation: Correct! By the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, $N$ must be prime or have a prime divisor. This is true for every integer greater than 1.
correct.insight: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic guarantees that prime factorization exists for every integer > 1.

incorrect.1: N might be prime or composite. We can't determine which yet, but it must have some prime in its factorization.
incorrect.2: That's impossible. Every integer > 1 has at least one prime divisor (or is prime itself).

currentState.expression: Case 1: $N$ is prime. Case 2: $N$ has a prime divisor $q$.
currentState.description: In either case, we'll reach a contradiction.

prompt.question: Why does this lead to a contradiction?
prompt.hint: If N is prime, it's not in our complete list. If N has a prime divisor q, is q in our list?

options.text: Either N is a new prime, or N has a prime divisor not in our list—both contradict our assumption
N must equal one of the primes in our list
N is both even and odd

correct.explanation: Excellent! If $N$ is prime, it's not in our list (since $N > p_i$ for all $i$). If $N$ has prime divisor $q$, then $q$ can't be any $p_i$ (we showed $p_i \nmid N$). Either way, there's a prime not in our 'complete' list!
correct.insight: This is the heart of the contradiction: we found a prime (N or its divisor) outside our supposedly complete list.

incorrect.1: No, N is larger than all primes in our list, and none of them divide N.
incorrect.2: This isn't about parity. The contradiction is that we found a prime not in our supposedly complete list.

currentState.expression: Contradiction: Our 'complete' list is missing a prime.
currentState.description: What assumption led to this contradiction?

prompt.question: What can we conclude from this contradiction?
prompt.hint: Our assumption that there are finitely many primes led to the contradiction.

options.text: There cannot be finitely many primes. Therefore, there are infinitely many primes.
The number N must be the largest prime
Prime numbers don't exist

correct.explanation: Perfect! Our assumption (finitely many primes) led to a contradiction, so it must be false. Therefore, there are infinitely many prime numbers. ∎
correct.insight: This proof is elegant: no matter what finite list of primes you give me, I can construct a number that reveals another prime not on your list.

incorrect.1: N isn't necessarily prime, and even if it were, we could apply the same construction again to find an even larger prime!
incorrect.2: We know primes exist (2, 3, 5, 7, ...). The contradiction proves there can't be a finite number of them.

currentState.expression: Proven: There are infinitely many primes.
currentState.description: This proof is over 2000 years old and still beautiful.

prompt.question: What makes this proof particularly elegant?
prompt.hint: Think about what the proof does and doesn't require.

options.text: It doesn't construct all primes, but shows any finite list is incomplete
It finds the largest prime number
It provides a formula for generating all primes

correct.explanation: Exactly! The proof's beauty is in its simplicity: given any finite list, Euclid's construction $(p_1 \cdots p_n + 1)$ guarantees we can find another prime. We don't need to know what the primes are or have a formula—we just prove the list never ends.
correct.insight: This proof technique (assuming finitude, then constructing a counterexample) is powerful and appears throughout mathematics.

incorrect.1: The proof shows there is no largest prime—that's the point! Any candidate for 'largest' can be used to find a larger one.
incorrect.2: Note that $p_1 \cdots p_n + 1$ doesn't always give a prime (e.g., $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 + 1 = 30031 = 59 \times 509$). It just has a prime divisor not in the original list.

keyInsights: Euclid's proof (c. 300 BCE) uses contradiction: assume finitely many primes
The construction $N = p_1 \cdot p_2 \cdots p_n + 1$ leaves remainder 1 when divided by any listed prime
Either N is prime, or N has a prime divisor—both cases give a prime not in the original list
The proof shows any finite list is incomplete, without needing to construct all primes
summary.fullSolution:
**Theorem:** There are infinitely many prime numbers.

**Proof (by contradiction):**

Assume there are finitely many primes: $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$.

Consider $N = p_1 \cdot p_2 \cdot p_3 \cdots p_n + 1$.

For any $p_i$ in our list: $N \div p_i$ leaves remainder 1, so $p_i \nmid N$.

By the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, $N > 1$ has a prime divisor (or is prime itself).

Case 1: If $N$ is prime, then $N \notin \{p_1, \ldots, p_n\}$ (since $N > p_i$ for all $i$).

Case 2: If $N$ is composite, let $q$ be a prime divisor of $N$. Then $q \notin \{p_1, \ldots, p_n\}$ (since none of the $p_i$ divide $N$).

Either way, we found a prime not in our supposedly complete list. Contradiction!

Therefore, there are infinitely many primes. ∎
